title: UNIFORMS — THE CLOTHES HAVE CLOCKED IN
dek: A visual WORK/LIFE essay about the portable org chart, plus a consent-first OPEN TO WORK board recovered from the useful core of Bosslist.
body:
Uniforms is the first standalone post in WORK/LIFE, on The Shift desk. It begins with a plain proposition: a uniform is an instruction written on a body. Before the wearer speaks, it can signal trust, availability, authority, belonging, protection, service, or disappearance.

Six familiar garments carry the essay: a hi-vis vest, scrubs, the black T-shirt, an apron, a blazer, and the name badge. These are PointCast editorial observations rather than universal claims about any occupation. A four-state local fitting room lets the reader ask what a uniform is doing—signal, protect, belong, or disappear. It changes page text and art, stores nothing, and makes no network request.

The visual system treats the post as a garment label and paper pattern: cream stock, cobalt work jacket, chartreuse safety panel, orange name badge, black cut lines, and a RETURN CONDITION: HUMAN stamp. Two generated images from Michael Hoydich's May 2026 Midjourney archive appear in an after-shift interlude. The archive did not contain a convincing uniform study, so the selected images truthfully show empty workplaces instead. They are labeled generated visual studies and are not presented as documentary evidence.

The companion OPEN TO WORK board recovers the durable part of an earlier Michael Hoydich concept called Bosslist. Archived notes described a Product Hunt for people: searchable vertical lists of specialists, jobs, recruiters, and visual profiles that gathered work scattered across the web. The useful core was the public list plus the opportunity layer.

This version is a privacy rewrite. It retains specific opportunity signals, proof before biography, and cards made for scanning. It retires silent indexing, contact imports, automatic profile crawling, up/down voting on people, and opaque human ranking. The public board begins with zero people because nobody is listed without an explicit yes.

A visitor can make a local OPEN TO WORK card with a name or handle, practice, desired role or project, place or time zone, one proof link, and a boundary describing work they do not want. Up to twenty-four drafts stay in that browser's localStorage. The author can copy portable JSON or remove the card. Nothing is sent, matched, applied, counted publicly, or published automatically. Opening the PointCast pitch door is a separate user-controlled action, and even a pitch is not guaranteed publication.

Together the essay and board ask two versions of the same question: how does work make a person legible, and how much control does that person retain over the signal?
